practice_items.atom_title: Password-attack signs (failed attempts, unusual times, unknown devices)
practice_items.prompt: An authentication log shows 47 failed logins for the same account over 90 seconds, then a success. What type of attack does this pattern indicate?
practice_items.explain: Rapid automated failures followed by a success is the signature of a brute-force or dictionary attack, not a human typing incorrectly.

practice_items.atom_title: Password-attack signs (failed attempts, unusual times, unknown devices)
practice_items.prompt: A defender sets an alert for '5 failed logins within 60 seconds for the same user.' Why is the TIME WINDOW included in the rule, not just the raw count?
options: To distinguish slow manual mistakes from fast automated guessing, reducing false positives
To allow clumsy users unlimited attempts if spread out
Because failed logins never accumulate more than 5 over a whole day
Because counting only works in 60-second buckets
practice_items.explain: Rate matters: 5 failures in 60 seconds signals automation; 5 failures over a week is normal user error. The window keeps alert noise low.

practice_items.atom_title: Password-attack signs (failed attempts, unusual times, unknown devices)
practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are recognized PASSWORD-ATTACK SIGNALS in an authentication log? Select ALL that apply.
options: Many failed logins for one account in a short time
A login from a device never seen before
A successful login at 3 a.m. when the user normally works 9-5
A user changing their display name in their profile settings
practice_items.explain: Failed-attempt spikes, unknown devices, and anomalous login times are the three key password-attack signals. Profile changes are not.

practice_items.atom_title: Password-attack signs (failed attempts, unusual times, unknown devices)
practice_items.prompt: Credential stuffing differs from a classic dictionary attack because:
options: It tries every possible character combination
It uses real username/password pairs stolen from a different service's breach
It requires physical access to the target device
practice_items.explain: Credential stuffing reuses breach data from other sites, exploiting password reuse across services. It does not try random combinations.

practice_items.atom_title: Password-attack signs (failed attempts, unusual times, unknown devices)
practice_items.prompt: An account lockout fires AFTER five failures. A defender notices the log has a SUCCESS before the lockout triggered. What should they conclude?
practice_items.explain: A success before lockout means the attacker found the correct password; the account is compromised and a full incident response is needed.

practice_items.atom_title: Weak authentication patterns; adversary dictionary construction
practice_items.prompt: An attacker has a 14-million-entry wordlist from a known breach. What type of attack does this enable?
practice_items.explain: A dictionary attack uses a prebuilt wordlist of likely passwords rather than trying every possible combination. Breach wordlists (e.g., rockyou.txt) contain the most common real-world passwords.

practice_items.atom_title: Weak authentication patterns; adversary dictionary construction
practice_items.prompt: Which of the following make a password MORE vulnerable to a dictionary attack? Select ALL that apply.
options: Using a common word as the base
practice_items.explain: Common base words appear in wordlists. Simple substitutions (a->@) and common appendages (word+'1') are covered by mangling rules. Long random strings resist dictionary attacks because they do not appear in any wordlist.

practice_items.atom_title: Weak authentication patterns; adversary dictionary construction
practice_items.prompt: The NIST SP 800-63B minimum password length threshold used in this course is:
practice_items.explain: This course uses 12 characters as the minimum (NIST recommends at least 8 for user-chosen, 12+ for production). Every extra character multiplies the search space exponentially.

practice_items.atom_title: Weak authentication patterns; adversary dictionary construction
practice_items.prompt: A password 'HelloWorld111' passes a complexity check (has uppercase, lowercase, digits). Which weakness flag does the automated checker still raise?
practice_items.explain: '111' is a run of 3 identical characters, triggering the sequential_or_repeated rule regardless of other complexity passing.

practice_items.atom_title: Weak authentication patterns; adversary dictionary construction
practice_items.prompt: Name the technique attackers use to automatically generate hundreds of variants from a single wordlist entry (e.g., 'password' -> 'P@ssw0rd', 'password1', 'PASSWORD').
practice_items.explain: Mangling rules (also called rule-based transformations) apply capitalization, substitution, and appendage patterns to each wordlist entry, expanding coverage without new creativity.

practice_items.prompt: According to NIST SP 800-63B, what is the primary driver of password strength?
practice_items.explain: NIST SP 800-63B explicitly moved away from mandatory complexity rules. Length is the primary driver because each additional character multiplies the search space by the alphabet size, while adding a new character class only multiplies it once.

practice_items.prompt: Which of the following are factors in a TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) computation? Select ALL that apply.
practice_items.explain: TOTP uses: (1) the shared secret K, (2) the current timestamp divided by the step to get the time step counter, (3) the 30-second step size. The user's password is a separate first factor and is NOT part of the TOTP computation.

practice_items.prompt: An attacker intercepts a valid TOTP code and tries to use it 45 seconds later. What happens?
options: The code still works because TOTP has a 60-second window
The server cannot tell the difference
The code works once more then expires
The code is rejected because the time step has changed
practice_items.explain: TOTP codes are only valid for the 30-second step in which they were generated. After 30 seconds the step counter changes and the server computes a different expected code. The intercepted code is permanently invalid.

practice_items.prompt: Name the two factors that MFA combines to protect a Wi-Fi login. Use the 'something you know / something you have' framework.
accept: something you know and something you have
practice_items.explain: MFA combines something you know (the password) with something you have (the authenticator app generating TOTP codes). An attacker needs both to succeed.
